The devices maintain stable operation under mechanical deformation and after 1000 cycles of repeated illumination. A lightweight neural network model is incorporated into the system to perform real-time spectral classification with high accuracy under varying illumination conditions. This work introduces a scalable, low-cost route to fabricating flexible, color-selective optoelectronic devices entirely through ambient, additive manufacturing.

title: Wide temperature range, ultra-extensible piezoelectric sensor for aircraft surface impact monitoring
abstract: Flexible sensors that can be laminated on curved surfaces are a desired form for aircraft surface impact monitoring. Sensors for such applications must withstand the wide range of temperature fluctuations on aircraft surfaces during flight and exhibit excellent extensibility to attach to and monitor large-scale curved surfaces, whereas existing flexible sensors fail to meet these demands. Here, we report a wide temperature range, ultra-extensible piezoelectric sensor. The sensor employs a flexible piezoelectric film based on polydopamine@barium titanate/cellulose as the sensing layer, enabling excellent temperature stability across a wide range from −50 to 80 °C. The tensile axial interconnects and horizontal connections linking external contact to sensor units, together with a sequential stacking process for the row arrays, enable the overall dual-axis extension of the sensor array with a strain ratio of up to 2500%. The ultra-extensible sensor array is attached to the aircraft surface to monitor impact signals continuously. Via an embedded impact localization algorithm, the response times of 25-channel impact signal data were analyzed to achieve localization of the impact. The ultra-extensible piezoelectric sensor with a wide temperature range holds significant practical value for monitoring unexpected impacts on aircraft surfaces, and will greatly advance the development of structural health monitoring technology for aviation equipment.

title: Multicolor electrochromic actuators for biomimetic skin-muscle coupling
abstract: Soft robotic platforms require actuators that integrate robust mechanical actuation with dynamic visual feedback; however, achieving muscle-like actuation alongside optical transduction in a compact form factor remains challenging. Here, we present a multicolor electrochromic actuator (ECA) that delivers large-strain, muscle-like contraction and RGB optical output by synergistically integrating a thermoresponsive liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) with viologen-based electrochromic ion gels. A transparent LCE layer embedded with a zinc-mesh heater enables reversible contraction via uniform Joule heating. Three laterally patterned, independently addressable electrodes support RGB ion gels, achieving crosstalk-free coloration with high optical contrast, reversible switching, and operational stability. Despite its thin, lightweight architecture, the ECA lifts substantial loads while providing tricolor visual output when mounted on robotic structures. This multifunctional coloration-and-actuation architecture embodies biomimetic skin–muscle coupling, offering a compact, adaptive strategy for soft robotics and wearable technologies.

title: Stretchable electroluminescent devices based on microLEDs: materials, fabrication, system design, and applications
abstract: Micro-light-emitting diodes (microLEDs) have emerged as one of the most promising emitters for stretchable electroluminescent (EL) devices owing to their high brightness, efficiency, operational stability, and environmental robustness. This review summarizes recent advances in microLED design, scalable integration, and strain-tolerant system architectures for mechanically reliable stretchable EL devices. Emerging applications in freeform displays and light-mediated healthcare are also highlighted, together with the key challenges and future directions.

title: Printed liquid metals for next-generation stretchable electronics
abstract: Liquid metals (LMs) combine metallic conductivity with fluid-like deformability, making them promising for stretchable electronics. However, their low viscosity, surface oxidation, and interfacial instability hinder precise printing and reliable device integration. This review examines how LM properties govern printing behavior, discusses modification strategies and methods spanning two to four dimensions, evaluates applications in stretchable electronics, and establishes material-process-performance relationships to guide future device design and practical manufacturing strategies.

title: Interfacial and mechanical engineering for scalable 3D integration of robust stretchable electronics
abstract: Integration of high-density multilayer circuitry in stretchable electronics is limited by mechanical instabilities at vertical interconnects and heterogeneous material interfaces. This work presents a strategy for monolithic 3D integration of robust multilayer electronics through synergistic interfacial chemical engineering and a “stiff-in-soft” structural design. Vertical interconnect access (VIA) utilizes a liquid-metal/plated-copper (LM/Cu) junction, where a self-limiting native oxide facilitates low-resistance Ga-O-Cu contact while inhibiting the formation of friable intermetallic phases. These VIA regions are further shielded from deformation by stiff encapsulation islands, achieving geometric integrity at strains up to 700%. Chemically active dual-network polyurethanes enable covalent and hydrogen-bonded encapsulating interfaces, ensuring solder-free contacts between LM interconnects and electronic components that preserve electrical stability during extreme deformation. The scalability of this platform is demonstrated by multitier photoelectric and wearable electronic systems that exhibit signal fidelity comparable to conventional rigid electronics. This methodology transcends the trade-offs between integration density and mechanical compliance, representing a new paradigm for the next-generation skin-like soft electronics.

title: Predictable conformal electronics enabled by a sliding-adhesion competition model
abstract: Achieving conformal attachment between flexible electronics and complex curved surfaces remains a fundamental challenge, as existing predictive methods are either computationally intensive or lack generality across arbitrary geometries. Here, we introduce a sliding-adhesion competition conformal model (SAM) based on differential geometry, which enables efficient and accurate prediction of conformability for arbitrary shape-surface mappings. By formulating a conformal factor derived from the first fundamental form of surfaces and incorporating interfacial adhesion and friction effect, SAM quantifies strain distributions and provides reliable failure predictions across diverse surfaces, while improving computational efficiency by 3–4 orders of magnitude compared to finite element analysis. Furthermore, the model offers the first quantitative insight into the superior conformability of high-aspect-ratio serpentine structures and supports high-precision inverse design of functional patterns such as antennas and sensor arrays, reducing placement errors to below 3%. SAM establishes a universal and scalable framework for the conformal integration of flexible electronics, with broad applicability in biomedical, aerospace, and soft robotic systems.

title: Curvature-adaptive low-temperature metallization for flexible and conformal electronics enabled by rheology-driven acoustic coupling
abstract: Achieving reliable metallization on curved and mechanically diverse substrates remains challenging because conventional post-printing sintering methods often produce non-uniform energy delivery, incomplete particle necking, and unstable electrical performance. Here, we report a low-temperature ultrasonic sintering strategy using a shear-thickening fluid-filled flexible bladder to improve conformal contact and rheology-regulated acoustic–mechanical coupling. Under combined external loading and ultrasonic excitation, the bladder transitions from a compliant state to a stiffened coupling state, promoting pressure transfer and ultrasonic energy delivery to printed silver nanoparticle films. Within 3 s of ultrasonic activation, the process produced dense conductive films with a conductivity of 2.51 × 10⁵ S cm⁻¹. The method was demonstrated on representative curved, rough, and flexible substrates, including UV-curable resins, eggshells, and polyimide films. When combined with five-axis conformal inkjet printing, the approach enabled continuous conductive patterns with low spatial variation across the tested non-planar geometries. These results provide a promising route for low-temperature metallization of flexible and conformal electronic structures.

title: A magneto-mechanical bio-interface with ultra-low-power analog backscatter for inclusive cardiac monitoring
abstract: Pervasive cardiac monitoring demands wearable systems capable of long-term, reliable operation across diverse users and environments. Modern optical wearables can provide accurate pulse-rate estimates, but performance can still depend on optical coupling, contact conditions, and device-specific sensing strategies. Here we report an ultra-low-power wireless bio-interface tag coupling magneto-mechanical cardiac sensing with analog backscatter communication. The tag transduces heart-induced skin micro-vibrations into magnetic-field fluctuations that modulate the reflection of an incident RF carrier, bypassing on-tag digitization and active radio transmission. Across 30 participants spanning Fitzpatrick skin types I–VI and diverse body weights, the tag maintained ECG-referenced RR-interval agreement and accurate heart-rate estimation relative to a commercial smartwatch benchmark under the tested protocol. The tag consumes 1.26 mW in active mode and 113.9 μ W under duty-cycled operation, enabling over five months from a coin cell. Multi-site monitoring during daily activities and hardware-in-the-loop EEG, EMG, and EOG replay further demonstrate extensibility toward long-term multimodal health monitoring.

title: Bioinspired Poisson‑actuated gating enabled high-sensitivity and stretchable multidirectional strain sensing
abstract: Decoupling strain magnitude and arbitrary orientation is a persistent challenge for wearable strain sensors, as conventional layered architectures and monolithic anisotropic networks suffer from issues of interfacial stress concentrations and irreversible signal drift under complex deformations. Inspired by the mechanogating mechanism of tactile sensory cells, we present a fluidic strain sensor with an orthogonal cross-shaped microchannel network and drum-shaped microstructures. The unique drum-shaped geometry exploits the Poisson effect to amplify transverse gap closure, inducing channel constriction. This mechanism yields a peak gauge factor exceeding 43,200 near gap closure—a four-order-of-magnitude enhancement over unstructured fluidic channels. The orthogonal architecture achieves intrinsic directional selectivity—the longitudinal channel elongates and narrows while the transverse channel shortens and widens—delivering a near-axial average directional selectivity of 15.42. By leveraging machine learning, the sensor achieves quadrant-resolved strain sensing with sub-2° angular resolution over 80% strain range, provided the loading quadrant is known. The fluidic transduction mechanism circumvents the mechanical fatigue inherent to solid-state sensing materials, demonstrating exceptional durability over 100,000 cycles. The practical utility is validated through table tennis stroke recognition achieving >95% accuracy, highlighting its potential for closed-loop athletic training and resilient human-machine interfaces.

title: Thermopower amplification in thermogalvanic cells via radiative cooling-mediated photothermal conversion
abstract: Emerging quasi-solid-state thermogalvanic cell (TGC) hold promise for low-grade heat harvesting. Harnessing solar energy to generate electricity through TGCs is limited by the challenge of maintaining a large temperature gradient (Δ T ) under illumination. Herein, we report an enhanced-performance photothermoelectric TGC by synergistically integrating localized photothermal (PT) heating with passive radiative cooling (RC), spontaneously establishes a robust ΔT on the bacterial cellulose-based TGC under illumination, enabling efficient photothermoelectric conversion. The flexible device featured an asymmetrically coated structure, employing carbon nanotubes and titanium dioxide as PT and RC functional layers. The optimized device achieved a Δ T of 14.11 K under 1 sun illumination, producing a voltage of 18.07 mV, substantially exceeding that of the PT-only counterpart. It delivers a maximum power density of 13.98 mW m −2 , a 214% enhancement attributed to effective suppression of parasitic heating. A practical outdoor application scenario was demonstrated, highlighting its potential as a self-powered device. As a proof-of-concept, the device has been developed as an intelligent light-control switch for smart windows aided by a voltage amplifier. By harnessing sunlight not only as a heat source but also as a trigger for asymmetric thermal management, this work achieves maximized Δ T in solar-driven TGCs, enabling a potential platform that integrates energy harvesting, environmental sensing, and responsive control.

title: Neuromuscular Junction Inspired Mechanosensitive hBN-based Memristors for Flexible Neuromorphics
abstract: Mechanosensitive neurons in neuromuscular junctions transduce bending into graded changes in synaptic strength, a biological design principle that artificial neuromorphic hardware has yet to exploit. Here, we demonstrate two-terminal mechanosensitive memristor with a vertical Ag/hBN/ITO architecture on flexible PET substrate, where its bending directly and reversibly programs synaptic plasticity through a non-destructive mechanism. Mechanical deformation drives interlayer sliding of the hBN flakes, perturbing the stacking and the inter-flake tunnelling distance without straining lattice. This programs synaptic plasticity, quantitatively mirroring the amplitude and dynamics co-modulation like in biological mechanosensitive synapses. Conductance states under varying bending conditions also serve as analog synaptic weights in a fully connected neural network trained on the MNIST digit-recognition benchmark, achieving more than 91% classification accuracy across all bending conditions. These results establish interlayer-sliding mediated tunnelling as a new mechanoelectronic design principle for flexible neuromorphic devices whose synaptic state adapts physical interactions with the environment.

title: Flexible, stretchable and sustainable paper electronics enabled by ultraviolet laser-induced graphene
abstract: The proliferation of short-lifetime consumer electronics has intensified the global electronic waste challenge. Paper, as an abundant and eco-friendly material, offers an attractive platform for sustainable electronics. Here we report a simple, additive-free, and ambient-condition approach to fabricate paper electronics by directly patterning laser-induced graphene (LIG) circuitry on lignin-rich kraft paper using a 355 nm UV pulsed laser. Under optimized conditions, the porous LIG electrode exhibits a sheet resistance of 147 ± 5 Ω sq −1 , a thickness of 43 µm, and an ablation depth of 20–30 µm, while maintaining stable electrical performance after 1000 bending or stretching cycles. We demonstrate paper-based LIG devices including flexible and stretchable electronic circuits, eco-friendly photodetectors, and electrothermal transducers. The compatibility of direct laser writing with roll-to-roll manufacturing provides a pathway toward scalable and low-cost production. These results establish paper-based LIG as a sustainable platform for flexible electronics, disposable sensors, and soft robotic systems.

title: Low-temperature monolithic integration of patterned distributed Bragg reflectors for high-resolution QD-OLED microdisplays
abstract: With the increasing demand for hyper-realistic displays, significant advancements have been reported in high-resolution quantum dot–organic light-emitting diode (QD-OLED) technology owing to its wide color gamut and improved color purity. However, achieving both high color purity and light extraction remains a critical challenge due to significant blue light leakage in high resolution QD-OLED. Here, we overcome these limitations by demonstrating a damage-free, low-temperature ( < 100 °C) monolithic integration of patterned distributed Bragg reflectors (DBRs) directly onto a QD-OLED stack to effectively suppress blue leakage and enhance conversion efficiency. DBRs fabricated from SiN x and SiO x using low-temperature ( < 100 °C) plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition demonstrate high reflectance of 95.9% at 455 nm while effectively suppressing reflectance in the red and green regions. A high-precision, one-step fluorine-based dry etching process achieved a 4 μm pattern size with a near-vertical taper angle of 89°, supporting pixel densities up to 3175 ppi. Compared to the device without DBR, the monolithically integrated architecture exhibits a photon recycling effect, enhancing red and green emission intensities by 19.7% and 10.7%, respectively, while reducing blue leakage by approximately 90%. Furthermore, the integrated device achieved a color gamut of 120.5% relative to the sRGB standard. These findings confirm that monolithically integrated DBRs serve as a robust and scalable solution for next-generation high-resolution QD-OLED displays.

title: A bio-inspired energy-resilient wireless skin
abstract: Soft and conformal wearable wireless systems are promising for healthcare, ambient Internet-of-Things and mission-critical applications, but persistent operation is hindered by mechanical deformation and fluctuating energy availability. Existing wearable systems are typically confined to fixed communication modes, relying on either energy-intensive active radios or low-power but functionally limited passive schemes. Here we present a bio-inspired octopus-like energy-resilient wireless skin (ERWS) with adaptive active–passive communication. The ERWS uses active communication for multimodal sensing and localization when energy is sufficient and switches to low-power backscatter sensing and data transmission when energy is limited. A time–frequency–space co-design enables this operation: undervoltage-lockout-based energy management controls temporal mode switching; dual-band operation assigns Bluetooth communication and radio-frequency (RF) energy harvesting to 2.4 GHz and wake-up/backscatter communication to 915 MHz; and a flexible optically transparent antenna, flexible solar cell and central functional island are vertically integrated. An island–bridge architecture mechanically decouples RF-sensitive components from stretchable interconnects, preserving electromagnetic performance under deformation. Experiments demonstrate autonomous mode switching, reliable active and passive communication, hybrid solar/RF energy harvesting, deformation tolerance and multimodal physiological monitoring, establishing the ERWS as an energy-resilient wearable platform for persistent operation under dynamic conditions.

title: Multiplexed sensor arrays for high-spatiotemporal decoding of complex physiological networks
abstract: Multiplexed sensor arrays expand biomedical interfaces by allowing independently recoverable sensing sources to share limited transmission, addressing, readout, acquisition, and computational resources. This Review compares time-, frequency-, spatial-, optical-, code-, and hybrid-multiplexing through a requirement–resource framework. We examine how signal integrity, front-end electronics, calibration, materials, mechanics, power, and data handling constrain source-specific recovery and outline architecture-selection principles for reliable physiological sensing and bidirectional biointerfaces.

title: Flexible active-matrix dual-band electrochromic display based on a Gires-Tournois resonator for human and robotic vision
abstract: Reflective displays have attracted considerable attention owing to their ultralow-power operation and compatibility with flexible and wearable platforms 1 . Although dynamic optical modulation has been demonstrated in reflective displays, including electrophoretic displays (EPDs), their operation remains confined to the visible spectral range. These spectral limitations restrict their applicability in environments that require reliable and simultaneous delivery of optical information to both human and robotic vision systems under varying illumination conditions 2,3 . Here, we introduce an electrically tunable dual-band Gires-Tournois (DB-GT) resonator integrated with a conducting polymer, poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):poly(styrenesulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS), realizing a dual-band active-matrix display platform that achieves simultaneous visible and near-infrared (NIR) modulation within a single active layer. By modulating the complex refractive index of PEDOT:PSS through electrochemical doping within a low-voltage range (−2.0 V to +1.0 V), the system achieves high reflectance contrast across dual bands, yielding a hue variation of ΔHue = 167.2° in the visible range and ΔR = 38% at 1270 nm in the NIR range, with rise time of 88 ms and a fall time of 165 ms. Furthermore, a 4 × 4 active-matrix pixel array fabricated on a flexible thin-film transistor (TFT) backplane demonstrates independent pixel-level control, supported by a high on–off ratio ( ≈ 10 6 ), low off current, and high spatial uniformity, collectively suppressing pixel crosstalk. The DB-GT resonator array is validated through visible–NIR dual-band recognition under bright conditions and robust NIR pattern recognition under haze and low-light conditions, demonstrating its potential for visual information delivery to both human and robotic vision systems.

title: Machine learning–driven structural optimization of zigzag silk fibroin ionic conductors for spatially resolved wearable motion detection
abstract: Flexible ionic conductors that maintain stable electrical performance under large deformation are critical for wearable sensing. However, their geometric design space couples topology, manufacturability, and deformability in a high–dimensional parameter space that trial–and–error approaches cannot navigate efficiently. Here, we present a data–driven structural design workflow for zigzag–patterned silk fibroin ionic conductors. Zigzag unit cells parameterized by four control points yield 3000 mirror–tiled variants whose biaxial unfoldability, quantified as the mean stretch ratio \({\lambda }_{{mean}}\) , is labeled by quasi–static simulations. An XGBoost surrogate trained on 15 structural descriptors predicts \({\lambda }_{{mean}}\) with \({R}^{2}\) = 0.97. A continuous–action A2C reinforcement learning agent then uses the surrogate to search for high–unfoldability configurations under manufacturability constraints. Three optimized configurations at \({\lambda }_{{pred}}\) = 1.27, 1.77, and 2.04 are fabricated as direct–write–printed silk fibroin ionic conductors with ten–channel resistance readout. Under cyclic joint flexion, the devices produce distinct spatial response patterns: the λ = 1.27 device shows a symmetric dual–hotspot distribution, the λ = 1.77 device concentrates response in one dominant channel (peak \(|\varDelta R/{R}_{0}|\) = 0.82), and the λ = 2.04 device achieves multi–hotspot coverage with the highest mean amplitude (0.27). Spatial fingerprints persist across bending speeds (Spearman ρ = 0.75–0.84), establishing a complete pathway from geometric parameterization through reinforcement learning optimization to experimental validation.

title: Light-regulated biomaterial interfaces enable flexible neural bioelectronics with stable adhesion and on-demand detachment for chronic electrophysiology
abstract: Dynamic bioelectronic interfaces are required to simultaneously ensure stable tissue integration for chronic recording and controllable debonding for device reconfiguration or retrieval. This challenge is particularly acute for implantable neural interfaces, where weak adhesion compromises signal fidelity, while permanent adhesion may cause secondary tissue damage during removal. Here, we developed a photo-programmable neural biointerface incorporating a self-healing bPDMS@Fe matrix based on a carboxyl-functionalized polydimethylsiloxane network dynamically crosslinked by Fe 3+ -carboxylate coordination. The resulting electrode exhibits robust adhesion to diverse substrates and biological tissues, as well as on-demand removal through UV-induced adhesion weakening. Moreover, it supports stable epidermal electrocardiogram recording under various conditions. Furthermore, the biointerface is translated into a 9-channel cortical electrode array that enables stable local field potential recording and spatiotemporal mapping of seizure-associated neural activity in freely moving mice. This work establishes a dynamic adhesive strategy as a new materials design paradigm for neural bioelectronic interfaces toward next-generation chronic electrophysiological monitoring devices.

title: Biomimetic functional materials, devices, and systems: integrating nature-inspired design across flexible electronic scales
abstract: Biological systems maintain resilience through structured and adaptive integration across materials, architectures, and feedback networks, yet flexible electronics arising from this often remain component-driven. In this perspective, we propose a system-level framework for biomimetic and bioinspired flexible electronics, linking nature-inspired materials, functional interfaces, and closed-loop architectures. Advances in tactile sensing, mechanotransduction, biointerfaces, and energy-aware computation provide promising routes toward autonomous, resilient, and biologically integrated electronic systems.

title: Liquid metal interfaces for component mounting on kirigami stretchable substrates
abstract: This study demonstrates liquid metal as an electrical interface material (LM-EIM) for mounting rigid electronic components on kirigami-based stretchable substrates. Kirigami structures impart high stretch tolerance to sheets made of materials with low stretchability through local bending and twisting. However, this advantage can be lost when rigid components are mounted using rigid EIMs, such as solder or conductive adhesive, because they mechanically constrain kirigami deformation and cause fracture at low strains. The LM-EIM itself exhibited high stretch tolerance, 24 and 35 times those of solder and adhesive, respectively. This highly deformable LM-EIM reduced constraints on kirigami deformation and suppressed fracture. Mounting with solder and adhesive reduced the substrate stretch tolerance to 32% and 36% of that without components, respectively. In contrast, mounting with the LM-EIM did not reduce the substrate stretch tolerance. The substrate fracture strain reached 3.99, corresponding to 1.1 times that without components. Finally, a resistor array maintained electrical connectivity up to a device strain of 2.0, while an LED array operated stably up to 1.5. This approach allows rigid, high-performance components to be integrated onto highly stretchable kirigami sheets without sacrificing their stretchability, enabling the development of high-performance, multifunctional stretchable electronics.

title: Adaptive tunable sensing system inspired by scorpions for dynamic vibration perception in unstructured environments
abstract: Embodied intelligence (EI) requires adaptive vibration perception that dynamically adjusts to target stimuli. However, conventional sensing paradigms with fixed parameters fundamentally limit EI from enabling adaptive perception for wide-range and unpredictable signals. Here, inspired by scorpions, which achieve adaptive and tunable vibration perception through a biological closed loop to reach an optimal detection state for variable vibration stimuli, we developed a Bioinspired Adaptive Tunable Sensing System (BATSS). The BATSS autonomously switches among three sensing states with distinct parameter configurations according to real-time signal variations, achieving an ultrahigh and tunable gauge factor of 17,889–29,558, a wide strain range of 0.012–2.83%, and precise discrimination of vibration amplitudes across a 500-fold dynamic range (0.04–20 g). Integrated into a hexapod robot, BATSS enables adaptive gait and posture modulation in complex terrains, achieving 100% traversal success with a 34.6% shorter traversal time. This work advances embodied perception for interaction with unknown environments and demonstrates strong potential for robotics where adaptability, robustness, and autonomy are essential.

title: Bayesian optimization-guided closed-loop morphology optimization of block copolymer blends via synchrotron X-ray scattering
abstract: The utility of block copolymers (BCPs) in next-generation nanofabrication and optoelectronics is strictly governed by the long-range ordering and precise periodicity of their microphase-separated domains. However, navigating their multi-dimensional processing space to maximize this structural fidelity can be difficult. Conventional optimization relies on Edisonian trial-and-error, which is resource-intensive, slow, and often fails to identify the global optimum. Here, we address this challenge using a closed-loop morphology-optimization workflow that integrates synchrotron grazing-incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS), automated scattering data analysis, and Gaussian process-driven Bayesian optimization (GP-BO). Applied to the swelling-induced assembly of poly(styrene-b-2-vinylpyridine) (S2VP) blends, the BO-guided closed-loop workflow explores the two-dimensional processing space defined by polymer blending ratio and solvent uptake. By jointly optimizing domain spacing and peak sharpness as a measure of structural ordering, the workflow identified target-satisfying conditions using approximately 30 experiments, more than two orders of magnitude fewer than required for uniform coverage at the stated resolution. Overall, we developed a constraint-aware acquisition strategy tailored to morphology optimization, in which domain spacing is treated as a feasibility constraint while structural ordering is optimized within the feasible region. This task-specific formulation differs from applying a standard GP-BO workflow and enables efficient navigation of a coupled landscape containing both monotonic and highly nonlinear responses.

title: Skin-mimetic adaptive gradient electrode for ambulatory noninvasive brain-computer interfaces
abstract: Noninvasive brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) need stable, comfortable electrodes for long-term wear. Current rigid or uniformly soft electrodes suffer from scalp mismatch, causing motion artifacts and short operation times. Inspired by human skin’s gradient structure, we created a skin-mimetic adaptive gradient electrode (AGE). Based on the Marangoni effect, we induced heterogeneous crosslinking in the hydrogel within a gradient temperature field. This yields an electrode with a gradual stiffness change—soft at the scalp interface and firm at the circuit connection—along with a gradient pore structure for sustained electrolyte release. This design enabled stable, high-quality EEG recording for over 8 h during free movement and over 14 h at rest, maintaining >94% typing accuracy. This work demonstrated the potential of gradient-designed hydrogels toward noninvasive BCIs in freely moving practicality.

title: Wireless monolithic flexible zinc-ion battery–pressure sensor enabled by a tough anti-freezing hydrogel electrolyte
abstract: Developing wearable sensors that integrate self-powering capability, reliable static and dynamic pressure detection, and miniaturized wireless signal processing remains a formidable challenge. Here, we propose a material–device–system co-design strategy to construct an untethered, all-weather, monolithic flexible zinc-ion battery–pressure sensor enabled by a tough anti-freezing hydrogel, a co-anode architecture, and a miniaturized wireless module. At the material level, a tough, anti-freezing PAM/CMCS-DMSO-Zn hydrogel serves as the core. It combines a low freezing point, superior toughness, fatigue resistance, and high ionic conductivity, enabling a dual role as an active pressure-sensing layer and a stable battery electrolyte. At the device level, a nylon-mesh-spaced co-anode architecture isolates the hydrogel from the Zn anode at rest, establishing a zero-output state that eliminates standby power. Upon loading, interfacial impedance modulation ensures static and dynamic pressure detection with rapid response and recovery times of 20 and 30 ms, respectively. At the system level, integrating the device with a custom printed circuit board creates an end-to-end microsystem for signal acquisition, processing, and wireless transmission, which we successfully validated across diverse harsh conditions. Ultimately, this co-design bridges hydrogel chemistry under extreme conditions with self-powered wearable electronics, providing a versatile paradigm for all-weather, wireless IoT sensing nodes.

title: Machine-knitted magnetoactive textiles for wireless charging, biomechanical sensing, and haptic feedback
abstract: A central goal of wearable computing is to understand and augment human physical interactions. This requires equipping wearable devices with functionalities such as wireless charging, biomechanical sensing, and haptic feedback. Most wearable devices integrate each of these functions separately with specialized components, which limits the device’s overall flexibility, comfort, and scalability. Here we present machine-knitted magnetoactive textiles that unify the physical mechanisms of wireless power transfer, biomechanical sensing, and haptic feedback in a single soft architecture. By coupling extruded magnetic fibers with digitally machine-knitted electromagnets, we enable functional textile transducers that can stably charge a 7.4 V battery, sense body movements up to 3000 Hz, and provide perceivable haptic forces up to 4.2 mN. We demonstrate how these transducers can seamlessly integrate into garments for applications like smart home control, motor rehabilitation, and skill acquisition, establishing a foundation for multifunctional wearable interfaces that are intrinsically compatible with everyday clothing.
